Nietzsche - Genealogy of Morals, Thus Spoke Z, Beyond Good and Evil (there's really no substitute for reading the primary translations; his prose is eccentric as hell, but some of the best in the tradition)

Husserl - Husserl's Phenomenology by Dan Zahavi

Heidegger - Being-in-the-World by Hubert Dreyfus (there are other, gentler introductions to Heidegger if need be)

Maurice Marleau Ponty - Phenomenology of Perception, Signs

To get a better feeling for Baudrillard, some other Frenchies might be of assistance, such as Sartre and Camus; although I am not a fan of many of the other post-structuralists.

Wittgenstein - Logical Investigations

John Russon - Human Experience

[For phenomenology to really strike you at all, it would probably help to have a general introduction to both philosophy and western philosophy specifically. I cannot recommend a great intro to the western tradition. I personally read Bertrand Russel's History of Western Philosophy and The Problems of Philosophy. These come from a distinctly analytic tradition, however, and the books I've recommended above deviated from this tradition, so bear in mind that phenomenology is a different mode of philosophy than what you think of happening in western universities today, for the most part. One other great introduction to philosophy in general that I would highly recommend would be Neil Tennant's Introducing Philosophy. To really get a feel for the divide that occurred between the analytic and continental traditions, you'd be advised to go back further and read the major empiricist, David Hume, and the idealists Kant and Hegel. I have no preference whether you go primary or read modern commentaries on these.]
